name: SpriteFlow
tagline: Browser tool for assembling, previewing and exporting sprite sheet animations for game engines.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Sprite sheet work is file math: pack frames into a grid or atlas, emit coordinates, play them back at a chosen frame rate. None of that needs a server, an account, or anyone else's data. An agent can give you a local canvas app with a timeline, onion skinning, per-frame timing and exports to PNG plus a JSON atlas in Phaser or Godot shape in a single sitting. What you will not get for free is the fussy stuff: trimmed-whitespace packing heuristics, pivot editing, and an export format for every engine you have never heard of. If you ship pixel art daily that polish gap is real, and if you touch sprites twice a year it is invisible.
coreLoopDIY: Drop a folder of frames in, reorder them on a timeline, scrub the preview at a set FPS, and export a packed sheet plus a JSON atlas.
requirements: Node 20 plus for the dev server
Your frames as PNGs, or an existing sheet with a known grid size
whatYouLose: Smart atlas packing: trimming transparent padding, rotation, power-of-two constraints
Export presets for engines beyond the one or two you hardcode
Pivot and hitbox editing per frame
Shared links and team review of an animation before it ships
Someone else maintaining the thing when an engine changes its atlas schema
moatNotes: The moat here is export breadth and the hundred tiny editor affordances, not anything structural. Neither survives contact with a user who only needs one engine.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because it already works and their frames are already in it. A sprite tool is a thing you open mid-task, annoyed, with a deadline, and a paid one that has already solved trimming, pivots and Unity export is worth more than a weekend you would rather spend on the actual game. The people who stop paying are the ones who settled on a single engine and a single workflow, at which point a 300-line local tool does the job and never changes under them.
notes: Image-in, image-out tools with no account are usually the easiest category on this site to replace.
prompt:
Build a local-only sprite sheet animation tool. No backend, no accounts, no telemetry, no network calls at all.

Stack, non-negotiable: Vite + React + TypeScript, plain CSS, HTML canvas for all rendering. No UI component library. No state library, useState and useReducer only.

Everything runs in the browser. Files are read with the File System Access API where available, with a drag-and-drop plus file input fallback. Nothing is uploaded.

Features that must work:
1. Import mode A: drop a set of PNG frames, sorted by filename with natural number ordering.
2. Import mode B: drop one existing sheet image, enter cell width, cell height, margin and spacing, and slice it into frames.
3. A frame strip at the bottom: thumbnails, drag to reorder, click to select, delete, duplicate.
4. A preview canvas that plays the animation on a loop. Controls: play/pause, FPS input (1 to 60), step forward, step back, loop toggle, and a zoom selector with nearest-neighbor scaling so pixel art stays crisp.
5. Per-frame hold duration in frames, defaulting to 1, editable on the selected frame.
6. Onion skinning: show the previous and next frame at 25 percent opacity behind the current one, toggleable.
7. Named animations: group subsets of the frame list into named clips, switch between them.

Export, all client side:
- A packed PNG sheet, uniform grid, columns configurable, drawn to an offscreen canvas and downloaded via a blob.
- A JSON atlas in Phaser 3 texture atlas format.
- A JSON atlas in a simple generic format: frame name, x, y, w, h, duration.
- A GIF is out of scope. Say so in the UI rather than half-building it.

Explicitly out of scope: trimming transparent padding, rotated packing, pivot editing, Unity and Godot resource files, any cloud sync.

Persist the current project to IndexedDB on every change so a refresh does not lose work, and add a Clear project button.

Ship a README with run instructions and a one-paragraph list of what this does not do.
